title: Independent and Joint Prospective Associations of Screen Time and Sleep Disturbance with Body Mass Index and Waist Circumference Among U.S. Adolescents
authors: Al-Shoaibi AA, Helmer CK, Shim J, Choi W, Dooley EE, Gooding HC, Pettee Gabriel K, Baker FC, Nagata JM

primary_models.name: Weighted multivariable linear regression of year-2 BMI percentile and WC percentile on baseline socializing screen time (texting + video chat + social media), adjusted for baseline BMI/WC percentile, puberty and sociodemographics, overall and stratified by sex
primary_models.location_in_paper: Supplementary Table 6 (BMI) and Supplementary Table 7 (WC) in the separate supplementary appendix (docs/pdfs/10.1089_chi.2025.0022_supplement.docx; not bundled in the 20-page author-manuscript PDF). Subtype analysis described in Statistical Analysis (p. 4); referred to in Results (p. 6) as 'consistent with the main findings'. The Discussion (p. 6) singles out TV/movies and video games as 'particularly associated' and does not discuss socializing.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal cohort. Socializing screen time is measured once at ABCD baseline (2016-2018, ages 9-10). The outcome is a single follow-up value at the year-2 visit (BMI percentile in one model, WC percentile in the other), with the baseline percentile of the same measure entered as a covariate, so the coefficient is the association with year-2 adiposity net of baseline adiposity. No repeated measures. Screen time x sleep interaction terms were tested for the main total-screen-time models and reported as nonsignificant (p. 4); no interaction tests are reported for the subtype models. The subtype models are reported for the whole sample and separately for females and males.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study (data release not stated). N = 7,445 participants with complete baseline screen time, sleep disturbance and sleep duration and year-2 BMI and WC (Methods p. 3; Table 1 p. 17); Supplementary Table 1 gives the included group as N = 7,455 and the excluded group as N = 4,516. COVID-19 reduced year-2 anthropometric collection. Implausible anthropometrics excluded (BMI z <= -4 or >= 8 SD; WC z < -4 or > 4 SD). Missing covariates imputed (puberty 16.3%, income 7.6%, baseline BMI percentile 0.4%, parent education 0.2%, physical activity 0.1%; Supplementary S4). 3,511 females (47.3%) and 3,934 males; mean age 9.9 (SD 0.6). Weighted race/ethnicity: 5.9% Asian, 16.6% Black, 16.2% Latino/Hispanic, 3.5% Native American, 56.5% White, 1.3% Other; 57.0% household income < $75,000; 85.3% parent with college education or more (Table 1, p. 17). The sex-stratified columns use the female (n = 3,511) and male (n = 3,934) subsamples.
primary_models.iv: Baseline socializing screen time, one of three screen-time types the authors derived from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey (TV shows/movies, video games, socializing). Socializing is defined as texting, video chatting (e.g., Skype, FaceTime) and social media (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter) (p. 3; Supplementary S2), so it is built only from phone/SM items and qualifies under FT-IC2 as a phone/SM-exclusive composite. Daily screen time was computed as [(weekday x 5) + (weekend x 2)] / 7 hours (Supplementary S2). The paper does not state the coding of the subtype explicitly; given that total screen time was entered as continuous hours/day, socializing is most likely continuous hours/day, so B would be per 1 hour/day. No mean or SD for socializing time is reported anywhere in the paper or supplement (Table 1 gives only total daily screen time, 3.7 h, SD 2.9).
primary_models.dv: Two continuous year-2 outcomes, modeled separately: (1) BMI percentile, computed from the mean of three measured weights and heights against CDC age- and sex-specific references; (2) waist circumference percentile, the mean of two WC measurements (inches, nearest 0.1) converted to percentiles using NHANES III reference data via the R package childsds (Supplementary S2). The footnotes of Supplementary Tables 6 and 7 state that the dependent variable is BMI percentile and WC percentile, and Supplementary S3 says baseline BMI and WC percentiles were the adjustment covariates. The main text and Table 1 instead describe BMI (kg/m^2; year-2 mean 20.6, SD 4.9) and WC (year-2 mean 28.8, SD 4.9), but those raw-unit descriptives do not appear to be the modeled scale. Year-2 percentile SDs are not reported; baseline percentile SDs for the included sample are BMI percentile 61.8 (SD 30.3) and WC percentile 61.1 (SD 29.0) (Supplementary Table 1).

primary_models.equation: Y2_pct[i] = b0 + b1*socializing_hours[i] + b2*baseline_pct[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*income + b15*parent_ed + b16*physical_activity + b17..*study_site + b..*pubertal_status + e[i], where Y2_pct is year-2 BMI percentile or year-2 WC percentile (separate models) and b1 is the focal estimate. Sex term omitted in the female and male models. The supplement does not say whether TV/movies and video games (or the sleep variables, which the S6/S7 footnote mentions) enter the same model as socializing.
primary_models.estimation: Weighted multivariable linear regression in Stata 18, using American Community Survey-based propensity weights and study sites as clusters in the survey procedures (Supplementary S1, S5). Missing covariate data handled by multiple imputation by chained equations, 10 imputed datasets pooled (Supplementary S4). Regression assumptions reported as tested and met. alpha = 0.05; no multiple-comparison correction. Sex-stratified estimates reported alongside the overall model; no formal sex x socializing interaction test reported. Complete-case sensitivity analyses (Supplementary Tables 8-13) cover total screen time and the joint categories only, not the subtypes.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: beta_std = B * SD_IV / SD_DV; d = 2 * beta_std / sqrt(1 - beta_std^2) (Borenstein et al. 2009 eq 7.1)
d_transformation.contrast_type: Per 1 unit of baseline socializing screen time, presumably 1 hour/day (coding of the subtype not stated explicitly)
d_transformation.notes: Not convertible because SD_IV is missing: neither the main text nor the supplement reports a mean or SD for socializing screen time (Table 1, p. 17 gives only total daily screen time, 3.7 h, SD 2.9, which cannot stand in for the subtype). On SD_DV: the Supplementary Table 6/7 footnotes and Supplementary S2/S3 indicate the modeled outcomes are BMI percentile and WC percentile, not raw BMI (kg/m^2) or WC. I therefore did not use the Table 1 year-2 raw-unit SDs (BMI 4.9, WC 4.9). Year-2 percentile SDs are not reported; as the closest available values I entered the baseline percentile SDs for the included sample from Supplementary Table 1 (BMI percentile SD 30.3; WC percentile SD 29.0) for the overall columns only, and left the sex-specific SDs null. If an SD for socializing hours becomes available (e.g., from ABCD baseline data for this sample), the overall cells could be converted with these proxy SD_DVs. [complete pass] Re-read full PDF (pp.1-20) and supplement docx (S1-S5, Supp Tables 1-13): still no socializing mean/SD and no sex-specific percentile SDs; every native B/CI/p for M1 is already filled.

extraction_flags:
Things a human should verify:

(1) Outcome scale. The S6/S7 footnotes and Supplementary S2/S3 say the DV is BMI percentile and WC percentile, with baseline percentiles as covariates. The main text and Table 1 describe raw BMI (kg/m2) and WC. I treated the DV as percentile and dropped the earlier draft's raw-unit SD_DV of 4.9. In its place I entered the baseline percentile SDs for the included sample from Supplementary Table 1 (BMI 30.3, WC 29.0), as proxies for the overall columns only. The sex-specific SD_DVs are null.

(2) SD_IV. No mean or SD for socializing time is reported anywhere, so d cannot be computed and transformable is false.

(3) IV coding. That socializing is in hours/day is my inference, not stated by the authors.

(4) Model contents. The paper does not say whether socializing was modeled alone or together with TV/movies and video games. The S6/S7 footnote also lists the sleep variables as IVs, which may be copied boilerplate.

(5) Supplement error. The Video games row of S7 is identical to the one in S6, which looks like a copy-paste error. It does not affect the socializing rows.

(6) Sample size. N is 7,445 in the main text but 7,455 in Supplementary Table 1.

(7) Interpretation. The authors never interpret socializing directly. They say subtype results were "consistent with the main findings" and highlight TV/movies and video games. The male BMI cell is the only significant one (B = 0.77, p = 0.001).
